docs.title: Home
docs.text:
✦ PYLOS ✦

A framework for encapsulating Great Expectations within data pipelines

Pylos (pronounced "PY-los") is a data validation and profiling framework for data pipelines. It handles the operational work around Great Expectations: it manages configuration, dispatches across engines, decides what happens when validation fails, and reports results to pluggable sinks.

Pylos runs as a layer inside someone else's pipeline (Airflow, Dagster, or a plain script). It is not a pipeline, a scheduler, or an ETL tool. It is built for automated systems that run daily and report on data processing, not for interactive data exploration.

Pre-release

Pylos is under active development and has not reached 1.0. Until then the public API and the configuration format can change between minor versions.

  • Getting started

    A complete config, explained key by key, then run.

  • Concepts

    The pipeline, the failure policy and how reports are written.

  • Configuration

    The keys a config file accepts.

  • API Reference

    Every module, generated from the docstrings.

docs.title: What it adds over Great Expectations
docs.text: Failure lifecycle GX reports that a batch failed, but it will not move the offending file to a dead-letter location or record what happened. Pylos does both. Multi-engine dispatch The same declarative YAML runs on pandas, Spark or SQL. Profiling GX 1.x removed much of the profiling support that 0.x had. Pylos brings it back.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S(["Source"]) --> E("Engine")
    E --> V("validate")
    E -.-> P("profile"):::planned
    V --> K(["Sink"])
    P -.-> K
    V --> L{{"Policy"}}
    L --> A("Action on the Source"):::effect
    classDef effect fill:#6e56cf26,stroke:#6e56cf,stroke-width:2px
    classDef planned stroke-dasharray:5 4

Profiling and validation read the source the same way, run on the same engine, and write to the same sink. Profiling never fails, so only validation can trigger an action on the source file. Profiling is not built yet, which is why it is drawn dashed.

docs.title: What Pylos does not do
docs.text: Not doing Because Scheduling or orchestration It is a layer inside Airflow or Dagster Writing validated data out (ETL) The calling pipeline has a writer Data catalog or lineage A different product Alerting (Slack, email) Pylos returns the result; the orchestrator's failure callback alerts Exploratory data analysis It serves automated systems, not people browsing data An in-house expectation vocabulary GX expectation names pass through unchanged

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
How Pylos thinks about a run. The pages describe what the code does today, and mark what the design adds but the code does not do yet as planned.

  • Pipeline

    How a config becomes a run: the five layers, and the two verbs that share one pipe.

  • Failure policy

    How a failed rule becomes a decision, and a decision becomes an action on the file.

  • Reporting

    What a report holds, and how a run is identified.

docs.title: Failure policy
docs.text: Great Expectations tells you whether a batch passed. Pylos decides what that means for each file and what to do about it.

docs.title: 🚦 From severity to decision
docs.text:
Every expectation in a contract has a severity, and the worst failing severity sets the file's decision:

flowchart LR
    R(["Results for<br/>one file"]) --> C{"A critical<br/>rule failed?"}
    C -- yes --> F("failed"):::failed --> A("Run the<br/>on_failure action"):::effect
    C -- no --> W{"A warning<br/>rule failed?"}
    W -- yes --> WN("warned"):::warned --> L("The file<br/>stays put")
    W -- no --> PS("passed"):::passed --> L
    classDef effect fill:#6e56cf26,stroke:#6e56cf,stroke-width:2px
    classDef failed fill:#e5484d26,stroke:#e5484d,stroke-width:2px
    classDef warned fill:#f5a52426,stroke:#f5a524,stroke-width:2px
    classDef passed fill:#30a46c26,stroke:#30a46c,stroke-width:2px
What failed Decision What happens to the file A critical expectation failed The on_failure action runs Only warning expectations warned Left where it is Nothing, or only info passed Left where it is

Only failed touches the file. All three decisions are written to the report. See Decision.

docs.title: 🚫 A file Pylos could not judge
docs.text:
Some files never reach a decision. A corrupt file cannot be parsed, and an empty file has nothing to check. These are recorded with status: aborted, the error type and its message, and no decision.

The run carries on with the next file, so one bad file does not hide the others. What happens to the unreadable file itself depends on mode:

mode A file Pylos could not read decision (default) Left where it is, reported as aborted any_failure The on_failure action runs on it

The default keeps a read error from moving a healthy file. A file that is slow to arrive or still being written fails to read for a reason that has nothing to do with its data.

An empty file follows on_empty. A pattern that matches no file at all raises a FileNotFoundError before any file is read, and no report is written.

docs.title: 🔁 Order of work in a run
docs.text:
For each file the runner reads, validates, decides, acts and records, then moves on to the next file. When every file is done, it rolls the results up and writes one report.

flowchart TB
    subgraph each["For each file"]
        direction LR
        A("Read") --> B("Validate<br/>with GX") --> C("Decide from<br/>severities") --> D("Perform the<br/>action"):::effect --> E("Record the<br/>result")
    end
    each --> G("Roll up<br/>the run") --> H("Write the<br/>report")
    classDef effect fill:#6e56cf26,stroke:#6e56cf,stroke-width:2px

Planned: write the report before acting

The design writes the report before the file action. If that write fails, the files stay untouched, and a crash between the two leaves a trail in the report. The code does not do this yet. See Reporting.

docs.title: 🎯 Two verdicts for a run
docs.text:
One value cannot say "11 of 12 files were checked and all 11 passed", so every run carries two:

Field Values Question it answers run_status completed, partial, aborted Did Pylos do its job? decision passed, warned, failed, or null Was the data good?

run_status is completed when every file completed, aborted when every file aborted, and partial in between. decision rolls up the decisions of the files that were judged, and is null when none were. A run with one failed file and one passed file has decision: failed. See RunStatus and PylosResult.decision.

docs.title: 🔀 Two verbs sharing one pipe
docs.text:
Pylos validates a source against a contract, and it profiles it. The two differ only in the middle step.

flowchart LR
    S(["Source"]) --> E("Engine")
    E --> V("validate")
    E -.-> P("profile"):::planned
    V --> K(["Sink"])
    P -.-> K
    V --> L{{"Policy"}}
    L --> A("Action on the Source"):::effect
    classDef effect fill:#6e56cf26,stroke:#6e56cf,stroke-width:2px
    classDef planned stroke-dasharray:5 4

Both read the source the same way, run on the same engine, and write to the same sink. Profiling only reports and never fails, so only validation feeds the policy.

Note

Validation ships first. Profiling is planned for a later release, so it is drawn dashed.

docs.title: 🧱 Five layers
docs.text:
A config passes through five layers, from what the user writes to what gets recorded afterwards.

flowchart LR
    subgraph dry["A planned dry run covers layers 1 to 3"]
        D("<b>1. Declaration</b><br/>YAML + Jinja") --> S("<b>2. Spec</b><br/>Pydantic") --> P("<b>3. Plan</b><br/>list of work")
    end
    P --> X("<b>4. Execution</b><br/>engine + GX") --> O("<b>5. Outcome</b><br/>decide, act, record"):::effect
    classDef effect fill:#6e56cf26,stroke:#6e56cf,stroke-width:2px

Layer 2 is built to work without any engine installed, so a config can be checked without Spark. A planned dry run will cover layers 1 to 3 and stop there.

Great Expectations already does nearly all of layer 4. Pylos is mostly layers 3 and 5: planning the work, deciding what a result means, and acting on it.

docs.title: ✅ Great Expectations underneath
docs.text: Pylos wraps Great Expectations and leaves its vocabulary alone. Expectation names pass through unchanged, so expect_column_values_to_not_be_null in a contract is the GX expectation of the same name.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Every run that reaches a file writes a report. Pylos is meant to run unattended every day, so the report is what the next person or machine reads.

docs.title: 📄 What a report is
docs.text:
A report is one JSON document per run, written by the sink in the report section. Only the local file sink works today. A real report is shown in Getting started.

The run_id is the contract name and the pipeline id joined by a hyphen, so every run of the same pipeline has the same run_id, and the local sink replaces the previous report.

docs.title: 🔬 Anatomy
docs.text:
The report is a PylosResult. At the top:

Field What it holds pylos_version The version that wrote the report run_id <contract name>-<id> run_ts When the run started, in UTC results One entry per source file run_status Did Pylos finish its job: completed, partial or aborted decision Was the data good: passed, warned, failed, or null

Each entry in results is a SourceObjectResult:

Field What it holds status completed or aborted for this file source_object The file's path, size and timestamps row_count, column_count The shape of the data that was read read_duration_sec, validation_duration_sec How long each step took error_type, error_message Why the file aborted, otherwise null decision passed, warned or failed, and null for an aborted file expectations One entry per rule action What was done to the file

Each rule is an ExpectationResult. It repeats the rule's name, type, kwargs, severity and expectation_key, and adds the outcome: success, element_count, unexpected_count, unexpected_percent, and the first unexpected_values with their unexpected_index.

The action is an ActionResult. Its status is one of these:

Status Meaning completed The action ran and succeeded skipped Nothing needed to touch the file failed Pylos tried the action and it raised. The decision and the rules are kept

See ActionStatus.

docs.title: 📤 Sinks
docs.text: A sink receives the report. The local file sink writes <path>/<run_id>.json. GCS and BigQuery sinks are planned, and a config that names them fails at load.

docs.title: 📅 Planned: write-ahead reports
docs.text:
The design writes the report twice around the file action, so a crash cannot destroy a file without leaving a record. This is not in the code yet.

flowchart LR
    W("Row written<br/>before the action") --> P("PENDING"):::warned
    P -->|"action ran"| C("COMPLETED"):::passed
    P -->|"action failed"| F("FAILED"):::failed
    N("Nothing to do<br/>for the file") --> S("SKIPPED")
    classDef failed fill:#e5484d26,stroke:#e5484d,stroke-width:2px
    classDef warned fill:#f5a52426,stroke:#f5a524,stroke-width:2px
    classDef passed fill:#30a46c26,stroke:#30a46c,stroke-width:2px

A row still at PENDING would mean Pylos was about to act and never recorded whether it did. A file move and a database write cannot be made atomic, so that window cannot be closed, only detected.

The same design adds a caller-supplied run_key, so a retried run keeps its run_id, and an attempt_id that tells attempts apart. Table sinks would merge on the row's identity instead of appending, and a merge would never delete rows it did not match. See Planned keys.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A config file has six top-level keys.

Misspelled keys are not always caught

A key Pylos does not know is rejected at the top level, in source and in on_failure. Inside validation, report and each expectation it is ignored without an error, so severty: warning runs as critical and enabeld: true leaves Data Docs off. Check the spelling there.

Key What it holds Page id The pipeline's name, part of every run_id Getting started engine What reads the data. Only pandas today Getting started source Where the files are and how to read them Source validation The contract and the Data Docs setting Validation on_failure What happens to a file that fails On failure report Where the results are written Report

The smallest config that loads:

minimal.yml
id: orders_daily
engine: pandas

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders_*.csv

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: id

on_failure:
  action: ignore

report:
  storage: local
  format: file
  path: output/reports/

Every example on these pages is loaded by a test, so an example that stops matching the code fails the build. Examples marked as planned are the exception, because they show keys the code does not accept yet.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Key Default source.on_empty skip source.options empty validation.data_docs disabled on_failure action: ignore on_failure.mode decision expectations[].severity critical

id, engine, source, validation and report have no default and must be present.

docs.title: On failure
docs.text:
on_failure says what happens to a source file whose data was judged bad. It sits beside validation, not inside it, because it can also apply to a file Pylos could not read at all.

on_failure:
  action: move
  dead_letter: output/dead-letters/

If you leave the section out, the action is ignore: the file stays put, and the report still records what failed. A report is always written, so this section only controls what happens to the file.

docs.title: action
docs.text:
IgnoreMoveCopyDelete 
on_failure:
  action: ignore

The file stays where it is. No other field is needed.

on_failure:
  action: move
  dead_letter: output/dead-letters/

The file goes into dead_letter and the original is removed.

on_failure:
  action: copy
  dead_letter: output/dead-letters/

A copy goes into dead_letter and the original stays.

on_failure:
  action: delete

The file is removed. Nothing is kept, so use it only for data you can fetch again.

See IgnoreFailureAction, MoveFailureAction, CopyFailureAction and DeleteFailureAction.

docs.title: dead_letter
docs.text:
The directory that receives files for move and copy. It is required for those two and not accepted for the others. Trailing slashes are stripped, and an empty value or / fails at load.

On local storage the path can be relative or absolute. See RelocateFailureAction.dead_letter.

docs.title: mode
docs.text:
mode decides which outcomes make the action fire.

Mode A file judged bad A file Pylos could not read decision (default) Action runs Left where it is, recorded as aborted with the error any_failure Action runs Action runs

decision is the safe choice. A read error can be temporary, such as a file still being written, and any_failure would move a healthy file because of it. Choose any_failure when an unreadable file really should be quarantined.

on_failure:
  action: move
  dead_letter: output/dead-letters/
  mode: any_failure

In both modes a file that passed, or only warned, is left alone. See BaseFailureAction.mode.

docs.title: The storage backend
docs.text: A move, copy or delete needs a storage backend to touch the file. Pylos fills it in from the source section, so the action works on the same storage the file was read from. You do not set it. See RelocateFailureAction.backend.

docs.title: Planned keys
docs.text:
These keys are part of the design and are not in the code yet. Using one today fails at load, as each of the examples below does. They are shown for orientation and are not loaded by the tests.

The release numbers come from the roadmap and can move.

docs.title: Several reports and BigQuery
docs.text:
Planned for the release that adds BigQuery. report becomes a list, so one run can write to several places, and a table sink takes a write mode.

Planned
report:
  - storage: local
    format: file
    path: output/reports/
  - storage: bigquery
    format: table
    dataset: data_quality
    write_mode: merge # append | overwrite | merge
    merge_key: [run_id, source_object, expectation_key]

docs.title: Runtime behavior
docs.text:
Planned with GCS. A runtime section controls how an execution behaves, apart from what it checks.

Planned
runtime:
  checkpoint: 1 # write to every sink after each object; -1 writes once at the end
  is_continue: false # skip objects this run already recorded; needs a run key

run_key is not a config key. The caller passes it for each execution.

docs.title: A shared contract file
docs.text:
Planned with Jinja templating. A contract can point at a file that several pipelines share.

Planned
validation:
  contract: contracts/customer.yml

Jinja also brings {{ env_var('...') }}, so secrets stay out of the file.

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text:
Planned for a later release. Profiling records descriptive statistics over time.

Planned
profile:
  enabled: true
  sample:
    rows: 100000

docs.title: More engines and storages
docs.text:
Spark and SQL engines, and more storages such as S3 and BigQuery tables, are planned. A table source has no file_path or file_format, and no file action applies to it.

Planned
engine: spark
source:
  storage: bigquery
  project: my-project
  dataset: raw
  table: customers

docs.title: Report
docs.text:
The report section says where the results are written. A report is written for every run, so this section only picks the destination.

report:
  storage: local
  format: file
  path: output/reports/

The section is a single entry today. See BaseEngine.report.

docs.title: storage
docs.text:
Where the report goes.

Value Status local Works gcs Planned. A config that names it fails at load bigquery Planned. A config that names it fails at load

See LocalSink.storage.

docs.title: format
docs.text:
How the report is laid out. file writes one JSON document. table, for rows in a table, belongs to the planned BigQuery sink.

See BaseFileFormat.format and BaseTableFormat.format.

docs.title: path
docs.text:
Where a file report goes. If path is a directory, which includes one that does not exist yet, the report is written to <path>/<run_id>.json and missing folders are created. If path is an existing file, that file is overwritten.

report:
  storage: local
  format: file
  path: output/reports/

The run_id is the contract name and the pipeline id joined with a hyphen. A pipeline with contract orders and id orders_daily writes output/reports/orders-orders_daily.json. Running it again replaces that file, so the folder holds the latest run of each pipeline and not a history.

See BaseFileFormat.path and LocalSink. Getting started shows a real report, and Reporting describes its fields.

docs.title: Source
docs.text:
The source section says where the data is and how to read it. Pylos expands the path to a list of files and validates each one on its own, so a failing file never hides the others.

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders_*.csv
  on_empty: skip
  options:
    delimiter: ","

The fields are documented in LocalSourceConfig and, for the ones every source shares, FileBaseConfig.

docs.title: storage
docs.text:
Where the files live. It is declared, never guessed from the path, so a Windows path like C:/data/f.csv is not mistaken for a URL.

Value Status local Works gcs Planned. Not usable yet: with move, copy or delete in on_failure the config fails at load

A local path must not contain ://, and a GCS path must start with gs://. Either mismatch fails at load.

Planned: Google Cloud Storage
source:
  storage: gcs
  file_format: csv
  file_path: gs://my-bucket/orders/orders_*.csv

See LocalSourceConfig.storage and GCSSourceConfig.storage.

docs.title: file_format
docs.text:
How to read each file. The field is free text, but only csv is read today.

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders.csv

See FileBaseConfig.file_format.

docs.title: file_path
docs.text:
A path or a glob. Pick the shape that matches how your files arrive.

One fileEvery file in a folderA date pattern 
source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders.csv

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/*.csv

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders_2026-10-*.csv

If the pattern matches no file at all, the run stops with a FileNotFoundError and no report is written. That is different from a file that matches and has no rows, which is what on_empty controls.

See FileBaseConfig.file_path.

docs.title: on_empty
docs.text:
What it means when a file has a header but no rows. An empty file passes every column expectation, so Pylos cannot tell a quiet day from a broken export. You declare which one this pipeline expects.

Value What happens to the empty file skip (default) The file is left alone and recorded as completed with no decision fail The file is recorded as aborted and the on_failure action runs on it SkipFail 
source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders_*.csv
  on_empty: skip

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders_*.csv
  on_empty: fail

See FileBaseConfig.on_empty.

docs.title: options
docs.text:
Reader options, passed straight to pd.read_csv. Pylos does not interpret them, so anything pandas accepts works, and pandas rejects what it does not.

source:
  storage: local
  file_format: csv
  file_path: data/orders_*.csv
  options:
    delimiter: ";"
    encoding: latin-1
    parse_dates: [created_at]

parse_dates matters when a date rule such as expect_column_values_to_be_between should compare dates, not strings.

See FileBaseConfig.options.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The validation section holds the contract, which is the list of rules every source file must satisfy, and the optional Great Expectations Data Docs.

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: id
  data_docs:
    enabled: false

The YAML key is validation. The fields are documented in GXConfig.

docs.title: contract
docs.text:
The rules for one dataset.

Field Required What it does name yes The contract's name. Appears in the report's run_id description no Free text about the contract's purpose expectations yes The list of rules

name is the YAML spelling of data_asset_name. Great Expectations also needs a datasource, a batch definition and a suite name. Pylos derives them from name as <name>_source, <name>_batch and <name>_suite, and you can override them with datasource_name, batch_definition_name and expectation_suite_name. Most contracts never need to.

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    description: Rules every daily orders file must satisfy.
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: id

See ContractConfig.

docs.title: expectations
docs.text:
Each entry is one rule.

Field Required Default What it does expectation_type yes A Great Expectations expectation name, unchanged kwargs no empty The expectation's own arguments severity no critical What a failure means. See severity name no <contract name>_<expectation_type> A readable name for the rule, shown in the report description no none Why the rule exists notes no none A free-form note, or a list of notes meta no empty Metadata carried through to the report

The default name is the same for two rules of the same type, such as not_null on two columns. Give such rules their own name to tell them apart in the report. Pylos also computes an expectation_key for each rule, a SHA-256 hash of its type and kwargs, and uses it to match each result to its rule. It appears in meta of the report. Setting expectation_key yourself fails at load, because the name is reserved.

Pylos does not check the expectation name or its kwargs when it loads the file. Great Expectations does that when the rule runs.

These are the expectations the project's own template uses, each with its kwargs:

Not nullUniqueRangeAllowed valuesColumn typeSchema 
validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: id
        name: id_not_null

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_be_unique
        kwargs:
          column: id
        name: id_unique

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_be_between
        kwargs:
          column: amount
          min_value: 0
          max_value: 1000000
        severity: warning

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_be_in_set
        kwargs:
          column: status
          value_set: [new, paid, refunded]

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_be_of_type
        kwargs:
          column: id
          type_: int64

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_table_columns_to_match_ordered_list
        kwargs:
          column_list: [id, amount, status]
        description: A column rename or reorder invalidates every rule after it.

See ExpectationConfig and the Great Expectations gallery for the full list of names.

docs.title: severity
docs.text:
Severity decides what a failing rule means for the file.

Severity If the rule fails critical (default) The file's decision is failed and on_failure runs warning The decision is warned. The file stays where it is info Recorded in the report. The decision stays passed and the file stays where it is 
validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: id
        severity: critical
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_be_between
        kwargs:
          column: amount
          min_value: 0
        severity: warning
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: note
        severity: info

See ExpectationConfig.severity and Failure policy.

docs.title: data_docs
docs.text:
An HTML view of the results, rendered by Great Expectations. It is off unless you enable it, and then nothing is written. Pylos's own report is the record. Data Docs is for people who want to browse.

validation:
  contract:
    name: orders
    expectations:
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null
        kwargs:
          column: id
  data_docs:
    enabled: true
    store_path: output/data_docs/

store_path is required when enabled is true, and omitting it fails at load. A relative store_path is turned into an absolute path at load, so it keeps pointing at the same place if the working directory changes later.

See DataDocsConfig.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
A Pylos pipeline is one YAML file. This page shows a complete one with every key that works today, runs it on two small CSV files, and reads what comes out.

Install

Pylos needs Python 3.11 or newer. It is published on PyPI as pylos-gx and imported as pylos, so install it with pip install pylos-gx or uv add pylos-gx. To work on Pylos itself, clone the repository and run uv sync.

docs.title: 📝 A complete config
docs.text:
Each numbered marker explains one key and links to its entry in the API Reference. The section headings in the explanations lead to the Configuration pages, where each key has more examples.

pipeline.yml
id: orders_daily # (1)!
engine: pandas # (2)!

source: # (3)!
  storage: local # (4)!
  file_format: csv # (5)!
  file_path: data/orders_*.csv # (6)!
  on_empty: fail # (7)!
  options: # (8)!
    delimiter: ","
    encoding: utf-8

validation: # (9)!
  contract: # (10)!
    name: orders # (11)!
    description: Rules every daily orders file must satisfy. # (12)!
    expectations: # (13)!
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null # (14)!
        kwargs: # (15)!
          column: id
        severity: critical # (16)!
        name: id_not_null # (17)!
        description: An order without an id cannot be reconciled. # (18)!
        notes: Added after the 2026-03 incident. # (19)!
        meta: # (20)!
          owner: data-platform
      - expectation_type: expect_column_values_to_be_between
        kwargs:
          column: amount
          min_value: 0
        severity: warning
        name: amount_not_negative
  data_docs: # (21)!
    enabled: true

docs.title: mode pydantic-field
docs.text:
mode: Literal['decision', 'any_failure'] = 'decision'

Which outcomes make this action fire. 'decision' (default, safe): only when Pylos read the file and judged the data to have failed (Decision.FAILED, a critical expectation did not pass). A file Pylos could not read or validate (RunObjectStatus.ABORTED) is never acted on: it stays where it is and the problem is reported instead, as status 'aborted' with its error_type and error_message on that object, and run_status 'partial' or 'aborted' for the run. 'any_failure': fires for Decision.FAILED and also for an ABORTED file. This can act on a file that never had a chance to be judged, for example a transient read error on an otherwise good file; choosing it means accepting that risk. In both modes a file that passed or only warned (Decision.PASSED, Decision.WARNED) is left alone.

docs.title: Plan dataclass
docs.text:
Plan(engine_id: str, engine_name: str, source: SourceConfig, contract: ContractConfig, on_failure: OnFailureActionConfig, report: SinkConfig, data_docs_enabled: bool, source_objects: list[SourceObjectMetadata])

What the run will do, resolved against reality, with nothing executed.

The config alone cannot say which files a run will touch, and the file list alone cannot say what will happen to them. Plan holds both, which is why it is worth rendering before a run instead of after.

Plan is a plain @dataclass, not a Pydantic model, although every field it holds (source, contract, ...) is a validated Pydantic model. Those models already ran their validators once, when the engine's YAML was loaded. A dataclass never re-runs them, whereas nesting a validated model inside another BaseModel can re-trigger its model_validator\ s unexpectedly. Plan only reads its fields: it is a snapshot, and only a test should construct one by hand.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION engine_id

The pipeline's stable id, shown in the header.

TYPE: str

engine_name

Which engine will read the data ("pandas", "spark", "sql").

TYPE: str

source

The declared source, for the pattern, reader and options.

TYPE: SourceConfig

contract

The rules that will be applied to every object.

TYPE: ContractConfig

on_failure

What happens to an object whose critical rules fail.

TYPE: OnFailureActionConfig

report

Where the report is written, whatever the outcome.

TYPE: SinkConfig

data_docs_enabled

Whether GX will also render its HTML view.

TYPE: bool

source_objects

What the glob actually found, sorted by path.

TYPE: list[SourceObjectMetadata]

Examples:

Planner.plan() normally builds it, but a test can construct one directly from fabricated data, without touching a real filesystem:

>>> plan = Plan(
...     engine_id="test_config",
...     engine_name="pandas",
...     source=source_config,
...     contract=contract_config,
...     on_failure=IgnoreFailureAction(),
...     report=report_config,
...     data_docs_enabled=False,
...     source_objects=[],
... )
>>> print(plan.render())

docs.title: ordered_expectations
docs.text:
ordered_expectations() -> list[ExpectationConfig]

Every rule, ordered by severity and then by declaration order.

This is the single definition of rule order. _rule_lines uses it to number --full-rules output, and anything else that needs "rule 4" to mean the same rule every time (a report, a log line) should use it too. It is public, with no leading underscore, so those callers can reuse it instead of re-deriving the order.

Both sort keys (a rule's severity and its position in self.contract.expectations) come from the config alone, never from anything resolved at plan time. So the order is deterministic: the same contract numbers its rules identically on every run and on every machine.

RETURNS DESCRIPTION list[ExpectationConfig]

Every expectation in self.contract.expectations, grouped by severity in the order critical, warning, info (_SEVERITY_ORDER), in declaration order within each group. The list is new; the contract's own list is not modified.

Examples:

A contract declaring [warning_rule, critical_rule] (in that order) returns [critical_rule, warning_rule]. Severity wins over declaration order, even though critical_rule was written second.

Note

To change the severity order (info before warning, say), edit the module-level _SEVERITY_ORDER tuple. Neither this method nor its callers hardcode the three names, so they all follow automatically.

docs.title: render
docs.text:
render(full_objects: bool = False, full_rules: bool = False, full_path: bool = False, timezone: str = 'UTC') -> str

Renders the plan for a terminal. This is the module's public entry point.

Everything else in Plan and the module-level helpers supports this method. A caller (a script today, a CLI --dry command later) only needs Planner(engine).plan().render(). It assembles the boxes and the object listing in a fixed order (source, objects, validate, rules, on failure, report, summary). Every argument controls verbosity only. None of them changes what the run would do, only how much of it this call prints.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION full_objects

List every resolved object instead of the first five (see _object_lines). For a future CLI --full-objects flag.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

full_rules

List every rule, not just the per-severity counts (see _rule_lines). For a future CLI --full-rules flag.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

full_path

Show each object's path exactly as stored instead of relative to the current directory (see _relative_to_cwd). For a future CLI --full-path flag.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

timezone

IANA zone name to render each object's modified time in, e.g. "Asia/Bangkok". It is the reader's preference, not part of the plan, so it is a render argument instead of a Plan field: the same Plan renders in whatever zone the reader asks for, without being rebuilt.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'UTC'

RETURNS DESCRIPTION str

The complete plan as one multi-line string, ready to print(). Every line is padded or bordered to a consistent width (see _BOX_WIDTH), so it lines up in a monospace terminal.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

timezone is not a recognized IANA zone name (a typo like "Asia/Bangkog", for example). The check runs at the start of the call, before any line is built, so a bad timezone never produces a half-rendered plan.

Examples:

>>> print(Planner(engine).plan().render())
  PYLOS plan · test_config · pandas

╭─ source ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  storage  : local                                                          │
...
  Plan: 1 object · 9 expectations
Note

To add a section (a future runtime box once checkpointing exists, say), write a Plan._runtime_box method like the others and call it here at the right point in the sequence. The existing boxes need no change.

docs.title: Planner
docs.text:
Planner(engine: Engine)

Turns a declaration into the concrete work a run would do.

It resolves the source glob, and it is the only part of a dry run that touches the outside world. It only lists: no file is opened, no expectation is run, nothing is moved and nothing is written, so a dry run has no side effect here to switch off.

Planner (which does the I/O) and Plan (the dataclass above, pure formatting) are separate classes. That lets Plan.render() be tested with fabricated data and no real filesystem, and lets the same resolved Plan be rendered several times (different timezone, full_rules, ...) without globbing again.

Examples:

>>> from pylos.loader import from_yaml
>>> engine = from_yaml("data/template_test.yml")
>>> print(Planner(engine).plan().render())
  PYLOS plan · test_config · pandas
...

Builds a Planner for one engine's declaration.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION engine

The loaded, validated pipeline declaration (usually the result of pylos.loader.from_yaml(...)). Planner does not re-read or re-validate it; config mistakes were already caught at load time.

TYPE: Engine

Note

self.backend is pulled out here only so prepare_source_metadata can read self.backend.glob(...) instead of self.engine.source.backend.glob(...). It is the same object as engine.source.backend, not a copy.

docs.title: prepare_source_metadata
docs.text:
prepare_source_metadata() -> list[SourceObjectMetadata]

Resolves the source's glob pattern against the filesystem, now.

This is the only I/O in the module; everything else in planner.py formats data that was already fetched. Two calls can return different answers, because a file can appear or disappear in between. That is why Plan is a snapshot: Planner.plan() calls this once, and every part of render() reports against that one list, so the numbers in a printed plan always agree with each other even if the filesystem keeps changing.

RETURNS DESCRIPTION list[SourceObjectMetadata]

Every object the source's glob pattern matched, as SourceObjectMetadata (path, size, modified time), sorted alphabetically by path. The backend's glob does the sorting, so the plan lists objects in the same order the runner will process them, and the five-object preview in Plan._object_lines is the same on every run.

Examples:

For source.file_path: "data/test_*.csv" matching three files, this returns three items sorted as test_1.csv, test_2.csv, test_3.csv, each with its own size_bytes and modified_at timestamp from the filesystem.

Note

What "glob" means for local files or a GCS bucket is decided by the storage backend (self.backend.glob, e.g. storages/local.py). This method only calls it, so it works unchanged for every backend that implements StorageBackend.

docs.title: plan
docs.text:
plan() -> Plan

Resolves the declaration into a Plan. This is the class's main entry point.

Other code (a future CLI, a test, the examples in this module) calls this method; everything else on Planner and Plan supports it. It does two things: it resolves the source's glob against the filesystem (prepare_source_metadata), and it copies every other field from self.engine unchanged, since those are declared, not discovered.

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Plan

A Plan combining self.engine's declaration with the result of prepare_source_metadata(). Call .render() on it to get the printable plan.

Examples:

>>> plan = Planner(engine).plan()
>>> plan.engine_id
'test_config'
>>> len(plan.source_objects)
1
Note

To resolve something else at plan time (checking that the report sink's directory is writable, say), do the work here and pass the result to Plan(...) as another field, the way source_objects is passed. Plan stays a plain snapshot of the result.

docs.title: pylos.policy
docs.text: Turns validation results into decisions: the verdict on the data, and what to do with the file.

docs.title: SourceObjectPolicy
docs.text:
SourceObjectPolicy(on_failure_config: OnFailureActionConfig)

Decides what a validation result means, and what should happen to the file.

Given the expectations checked against one source object, it answers the two questions the rest of the run needs:

was the data good?       -> Decision.PASSED / WARNED / FAILED
what do we do about it?  -> an ActionResult naming the action to perform

Severity connects the two: a failure matters as much as the contract says it does.

a critical expectation failed  -> FAIL, and the configured on_failure action is planned (move, copy, delete)
only warnings failed           -> WARN, the file is left where it is
nothing failed, or only info   -> PASS, the file is left where it is

Only FAIL ever touches the file. WARN and PASS are still written to the report, but they do not move anything.

SourceObjectPolicy is a brain with no hands. It never opens a file, relocates one, or writes a report, and it keeps no per-object state: decide() takes one object's results and returns the verdicts without storing them, so one instance could serve every object in a run. It can therefore be tested with nothing but a list of fabricated ExpectationResult objects: no GX, no storage, no engine, no I/O.

The ActionResult it returns is only an intent: its status is PENDING for an action that will run and SKIPPED when there is nothing to do. The report records that intent before the runner acts, so a row still at PENDING afterwards means the process died in between.

It looks at one source object at a time, never at its neighbours. The run-level verdicts (run_status, decision) are rollups computed over every object after the loop finishes; SourceObjectPolicy does not produce them.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION on_failure_config

What the config said to do with a file that fails.

Prepare a policy for one pipeline.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION on_failure_config

The pipeline's on_failure block, used only to choose the action for a FAILED object.

TYPE: OnFailureActionConfig

docs.title: plan_action
docs.text:
plan_action(decision_result: Decision) -> ActionResult

Derives the unexecuted action from a verdict and on_failure_config.

Only FAIL leads to a real action, and only when the config is not IgnoreFailureAction. Every other case returns IGNORE / SKIPPED, because nothing touches the file. The runner performs a PENDING action and updates its status afterwards.

This is public, not only a step inside decide(), because the runner also calls it directly for an object whose decision never came from expectations, such as a SourceEmptyError or an any_failure abort. It passes Decision.FAILED to select the action without claiming that verdict happened.

docs.title: decide
docs.text:
decide(expectation_results: list[ExpectationResult]) -> tuple[Decision, ActionResult]

Turns one source object's expectation results into its two verdicts.

This is the main entry point. The runner calls plan_action directly only for objects that have no expectation results to judge. Nothing is read, written or relocated here: the runner records the decision and then performs the action if one is due.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION expectation_results

Every expectation checked against this one source object, as produced by gx/.

TYPE: list[ExpectationResult]

RETURNS DESCRIPTION tuple[Decision, ActionResult]

The Decision for the object and the ActionResult the runner should carry out. Neither is stored on self.

docs.title: PylosPolicy
docs.text: Rolls the per-object decisions up into the decision for the whole run.

docs.title: decide
docs.text:
decide(source_object_results: list[SourceObjectResult]) -> Decision | None

The run-level decision: the worst decision across all objects.

docs.title: ActionName
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

What Pylos can do to a source file once on_failure decides to act.

Mirrors the action field of the on_failure config block one-to-one. The YAML author picks one of these four, and policy.py copies that same value onto the ActionResult it plans, unchanged.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION IGNORE

Leave the file exactly where it is. Also the value policy.py uses when nothing needs to happen at all, not only when the user configured it explicitly.

DELETE

Remove the file from its source location.

MOVE

Relocate the file into dead_letter, removing the original.

COPY

Copy the file into dead_letter, leaving the original in place.

Examples:

>>> ActionName.MOVE
<ActionName.MOVE: 'move'>

>>> ActionName.MOVE.value
'move'

>>> ActionName.MOVE == "move"
True

docs.title: ActionStatus
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Where one ActionResult is in its own lifecycle, separate from which action it names.

policy.py only ever produces PENDING or SKIPPED. The runner moves a PENDING row to COMPLETED or FAILED once it has tried to perform the action.

A row still at PENDING in a written report means the process died between planning the action and carrying it out.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION PENDING

The action is due but has not run yet.

SKIPPED

Nothing needs to touch the file, e.g. the decision was PASSED or WARNED.

COMPLETED

The runner performed the action and it succeeded.

FAILED

The runner tried to perform the action and it raised.

Examples:

>>> ActionStatus.PENDING
<ActionStatus.PENDING: 'pending'>

>>> ActionStatus.PENDING == "pending"
True

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Was the data itself good, for one source object or for the whole run.

Derived from expectation severities, not from whether Pylos managed to run at all. An object that could not be read has no Decision, because there was no data to judge (see RunObjectStatus.ABORTED).

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION PASSED

No expectation failed, or only info ones did.

WARNED

The worst failing expectation was warning.

FAILED

At least one critical expectation failed.

Only FAILED ever triggers the configured on_failure action. The other two leave the file untouched but are still written to the report.

At the run level, PylosResult.decision rolls these up across every object. It answers "is the data okay" for whoever owns the data. RunStatus answers a different question, "did Pylos do its job", for whoever runs the pipeline.

Examples:

>>> Decision.FAILED
<Decision.FAILED: 'failed'>

>>> Decision.FAILED == "failed"
True

docs.title: RunStatus
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Did Pylos manage to do its job for this run, independent of what the data looked like.

A rollup of every object's RunObjectStatus, not of their Decision. A run where every single file failed every expectation is still COMPLETED, because Pylos read and validated all of them successfully.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION COMPLETED

Every object completed, including an empty, allowed glob.

PARTIAL

A mix of completed and aborted objects.

ABORTED

Every object aborted.

ABORTED should draw attention before PARTIAL. When no object could even be processed, the cause is usually systemic (bad credentials, a network outage), not ordinary bad data.

PARTIAL is the everyday case of "partial failure continues": a few files could not be read, and the rest still ran.

Read by whoever runs the pipeline; Decision is read by whoever owns the data.

Examples:

>>> RunStatus.PARTIAL
<RunStatus.PARTIAL: 'partial'>

>>> RunStatus.PARTIAL == "partial"
True

docs.title: RunObjectStatus
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Did Pylos finish processing one source object, independent of the verdict.

Set once per object, before Decision is even known.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION COMPLETED

The object was read and every expectation ran, whatever the result was.

ABORTED

Something raised before that point instead, e.g. a corrupt file or an unreadable encoding, caught by the runner's try/except around the read and validate steps.

RunStatus is the rollup of these two values across every object in the run.

Examples:

>>> RunObjectStatus.ABORTED
<RunObjectStatus.ABORTED: 'aborted'>

>>> RunObjectStatus.ABORTED == "aborted"
True

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Pylos's own mirror of GX's FailureSeverity: same three levels, no GX import.

Building a GX expectation suite requires a FailureSeverity value (from great_expectations.expectations.metadata_types). results.py is a leaf module that imports nothing from Pylos or GX, so every other module can depend on it without pulling in great_expectations.

An equivalent enum here keeps that boundary. gx/validator.py's _map_severity is the only place that translates between the two.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION CRITICAL

A failure triggers the configured on_failure action.

WARNING

A failure is recorded but the file is left alone.

INFO

A failure is recorded as a note for a person, nothing more.

Examples:

>>> Severity.CRITICAL
<Severity.CRITICAL: 'critical'>

>>> Severity.CRITICAL == "critical"
True

docs.title: Runner
docs.text:
Runner(engine: Engine)

Runs one pipeline end to end: list, read, validate, decide, act, report.

For each source object the glob matches, the runner reads it with the engine, validates it with GX, asks SourceObjectPolicy for a decision and an action, performs the action, and records a SourceObjectResult. When every object is done, it rolls the results up into one PylosResult and writes it to the report sink.

One bad object does not stop the run. An empty source is handled according to source.on_empty, any other exception marks that object aborted, and the loop moves on to the next object. on_failure.mode decides whether an aborted object is acted on.

Examples:

>>> from pylos.loader import from_yaml
>>> Runner(from_yaml("data/template_test.yml")).run()

Prepare a runner for one loaded pipeline.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION engine

The validated pipeline declaration, usually from pylos.loader.from_yaml. Each source object is read into a copy of it, so this instance itself never holds data.

TYPE: Engine

docs.text:

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run() -> None

Process every source object, then write one report for the whole run.

For each object the glob matches:

  1. Read it into a copy of the engine and collect its statistics.
  2. Validate it with GX and translate the result into ExpectationResult rows.
  3. Ask SourceObjectPolicy for the decision and the action.
  4. Perform the action (see _apply_action).
  5. Record a SourceObjectResult.

How each kind of failure is recorded:

  • Empty source (SourceEmptyError): with on_empty: skip the file is left alone and the object is completed with no decision. With on_empty: fail the failure action is performed and the object is aborted.
  • Any other exception while reading or validating: the object is aborted, and the failure action runs only when on_failure.mode is any_failure.
  • The action itself fails: the object is aborted, but its decision and expectation results are kept.

After the loop, PylosPolicy gives the run-level decision, and run_status is completed if every object completed, aborted if every object aborted, and partial otherwise. The PylosResult is then written to the report sink; nothing is returned.

run_id is <contract name>-<id>, so every run of the same pipeline gets the same run_id, and the local sink overwrites the previous report file.

RAISES DESCRIPTION FileNotFoundError

With local storage, the pattern matched no file. The glob raises this before any object is processed, so no report is written.

docs.title: GXTranslateExpectationResult
docs.text:
GXTranslateExpectationResult(validation_config: list[ExpectationConfig])

Turns one GX validation result into Pylos's own ExpectationResult rows.

This class sits at the GX/Pylos boundary. Everything downstream of translate() (policy, sinks, reports) works only with Pylos's own ExpectationResult model and never touches a GX object. Every GX-specific detail (the nested result dict shape, the partial_-prefixed keys, the fact that meta is the only field that survives a suite round trip) stays in this one class. When a future GX version changes its result schema, the fix is a diff to translate() alone, and nothing else in Pylos needs to change.

GX's result dict carries no Pylos identifiers of its own. expectation_key survives the round trip only through expectation_config.meta; GX regenerates its own id when a suite is added to a context, so that field cannot be used. translate() uses the key to match each GX result back to the ExpectationConfig that produced it, then rebuilds the fields Pylos reports on. Some come from our own config (name, type, kwargs, description, severity) and others from GX's result payload (success, counts, unexpected values).

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION validation_config

The expectations that were validated, used to look up each GX result's declared name/description/severity by its key.

Prepare a translator for one contract.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION validation_config

The contract's expectations, in any order. Each GX result is matched back to one of these by expectation_key.

TYPE: list[ExpectationConfig]

docs.text:
translate(gx_result: ExpectationSuiteValidationResult) -> list[ExpectationResult]

Converts gx_result into ExpectationResult rows, one per expectation.

RETURNS DESCRIPTION list[ExpectationResult]

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

gx_result has no results list; an entry is missing expectation_key in expectation_config.meta; an entry's key matches no expectation in validation_config; or an entry has no exception_info. A missing key means Pylos's own meta injection did not survive validation, which is a framework bug, not a user error.

docs.text:
move_obj(src: str, dst_dir: str) -> str

Move a file into a directory, letting the OS perform the move.

Within one filesystem this is a rename and therefore atomic; across devices shutil degrades to copy-then-delete, which can leave the file in both places if the delete fails.

Note

The destination keeps the source's file name, so moving 2026-08-15/orders.csv and 2026-08-16/orders.csv into the same directory leaves only the second, silently, on both Windows and POSIX. Callers that dead-letter files from more than one directory should pass a distinct dst_dir per run.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION src

Path of the file to move.

TYPE: str

dst_dir

Directory to move it into. Created if absent.

TYPE: str

RETURNS DESCRIPTION str

docs.title: BaseStorage pydantic-model
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel, ABC

Interface for file operations on a storage backend.

One subclass per backend (local disk, GCS, S3), each implemented with that backend's own SDK. glob resolves a source pattern into the files a run will process, each with the size and mtime the planner renders. move_obj, copy_obj and delete_obj relocate or remove a file after validation fails.

Reading is not part of this interface: engines read by URI with their own readers.

Paths are URIs in whatever form the backend uses: filesystem paths for local storage, gs://bucket/key for GCS.

docs.title: glob
docs.text:
glob(pattern: str) -> list[SourceObjectMetadata]

Resolve a pattern into the objects it matches, metadata included.

A template method. The shape of the result is fixed here so every backend agrees on it: sorted by path for a reproducible processing order, with no directories. The order is a-z ignoring case, with numbers compared by value (test_2 before test_10). Backends supply the two halves: _list_files walks the backend, and _to_metadata turns one native entry into a SourceObjectMetadata.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION pattern

A glob in the backend's syntax, such as data/test_*.csv. A pattern containing no wildcard matches only itself.

TYPE: str

RETURNS DESCRIPTION list[SourceObjectMetadata]

The matching objects, sorted by path in natural order. Empty when nothing matches, which source.on_empty assigns meaning to.

Move a file into a directory, letting the OS perform the move.

Within one filesystem this is a rename and therefore atomic; across devices shutil degrades to copy-then-delete, which can leave the file in both places if the delete fails.
